COM747 Week 3 Seminar: Complete Solutions

Law of large numbers, power, the rundata tutorial, scientific notation and outliers

How to use this notebook. All four Week 3 exercises, completed and commented line by line, plus the short note on the tilde. Put rundata.csv in the same folder. Where a sheet’s code is misleading or fails, an orange box explains the fix.

library(pwr)      # install.packages("pwr")

Exercise 1: The law of large numbers

1.1 The sheet’s code, with comments

set.seed(52)                               # so your plots match these (not in the sheet)
population <- rnorm(1000, 52, 40)          # a "population" of 1000 exam scores: mean 52, SD 40
samplemeans <- vector(length = 100)        # empty vector to hold 100 sample means
sampleSDs   <- vector(length = 100)        # and 100 sample SDs

for (i in 1:100) {                         # repeat for i = 1, 2, ..., 100
  y <- sample(population, i * 10)          # draw a sample of size 10, 20, ..., 1000 (without replacement)
  samplemeans[i] <- mean(y)                # store this sample's mean
  sampleSDs[i]   <- sd(y)                  # and its standard deviation
}

1.2 Plots

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(samplemeans, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa6", xlab = "i (sample size = 10 i)", ylab = "sample mean",
     main = "Sample means approach the population mean")
abline(h = 52, col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)              # the true (theoretical) mean
abline(h = mean(population), lty = 2)                 # the mean of these 1000 numbers
plot(sampleSDs, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa6", xlab = "i (sample size = 10 i)", ylab = "sample SD",
     main = "Sample SDs approach the population SD")
abline(h = 40, col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)
abline(h = sd(population), lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Small samples (left) scatter widely; large samples (right) settle down. The spread of the sample means shrinks like \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\): the standard error.

A subtlety. sample(population, i * 10) samples without replacement from only 1,000 numbers, so at i = 100 the “sample” is the whole population and its mean is exactly mean(population) (dashed line), not 52. The 1,000 numbers are themselves a sample from the N(52, 40) distribution. To see the law of large numbers for the true mean, sample from the distribution itself:

set.seed(1)
n <- c(10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, 50000)
data.frame(n = n, sample_mean = round(sapply(n, function(k) mean(rnorm(k, 52, 40))), 2),
           standard_error = round(40 / sqrt(n), 2))
##       n sample_mean standard_error
## 1    10       57.29          12.65
## 2    50       56.11           5.66
## 3   100       49.72           4.00
## 4   500       51.66           1.79
## 5  1000       51.42           1.26
## 6  5000       51.89           0.57
## 7 10000       51.43           0.40
## 8 50000       51.92           0.18

1.3 Playing with the simulator

lln <- function(pop_mean = 52, pop_sd = 40, steps = 100, step = 10, dist = c("normal", "skewed")) {
  dist <- match.arg(dist)
  sizes <- (1:steps) * step
  means <- sapply(sizes, function(k) mean(if (dist == "normal") rnorm(k, pop_mean, pop_sd) else rexp(k, 1 / pop_mean)))
  plot(sizes, means, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa6", xlab = "sample size", ylab = "sample mean",
       main = paste("Law of large numbers:", dist, "population"))
  abline(h = pop_mean, col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)
}
set.seed(2); lln(pop_sd = 5)            # small SD: means settle quickly

set.seed(2); lln(dist = "skewed")       # still works for a skewed (exponential) population

Exercise 2: Simulation, effect size and power

2.1 The simulation, commented

set.seed(3)
samplesize <- 200                 # sample size of EACH group
meanX <- 50; meanY <- 51          # population means: a true difference of 1
sdX <- 5;    sdY <- 5             # population SDs
pvalues <- vector(length = 100)

effectSize <- abs(meanX - meanY) / sqrt(((sdX * sdX) + (sdY * sdY)) / 2)   # Cohen's d = difference / pooled SD
effectSize                        # 0.2: a "small" effect
## [1] 0.2
for (i in 1:100) {                # 100 independent studies
  x <- rnorm(samplesize, meanX, sdX)      # each study samples both groups
  y <- rnorm(samplesize, meanY, sdY)
  p <- t.test(x, y)                       # Welch two-sample t-test
  pvalues[i] <- p$p.value
}
hist(pvalues, breaks = 20, col = "#cfdcf0", main = "p-values from 100 studies")
abline(v = 0.05, col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)

length(pvalues[pvalues < 0.05])   # studies that detected the (real) difference: about the power
## [1] 48

The sheet writes t.test(x, y, PAIRED = FALSE). R is case-sensitive, so PAIRED isn’t the paired argument: it is silently ignored. The result is still an unpaired test only because that is the default. Write paired = FALSE if you mean it.

2.2 Manipulate the variables: power curves

sim_power <- function(n, d, reps = 300) {
  mean(replicate(reps, t.test(rnorm(n, 0, 1), rnorm(n, d, 1))$p.value < 0.05))
}
set.seed(4)
grid <- expand.grid(n = c(10, 20, 50, 100, 200), d = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8))
grid$power <- mapply(sim_power, grid$n, grid$d)
xtabs(power ~ n + d, grid)
##      d
## n            0.2        0.5        0.8
##   10  0.08333333 0.16333333 0.39000000
##   20  0.09000000 0.36000000 0.67000000
##   50  0.16333333 0.72333333 0.97666667
##   100 0.30000000 0.94000000 1.00000000
##   200 0.46666667 1.00000000 1.00000000
cols <- c("#2b5fa6", "#d0791a", "#2f7d5b")
plot(NULL, xlim = c(10, 200), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "sample size per group", ylab = "power",
     main = "Simulated power by effect size")
for (j in seq_along(unique(grid$d))) { g <- grid[grid$d == unique(grid$d)[j], ]; lines(g$n, g$power, type = "b", col = cols[j], pch = 19, lwd = 2) }
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("d =", unique(grid$d)), col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

Bigger effects and bigger samples both raise power. A small effect (d = 0.2) needs about 400 per group for 80% power.

2.3 R’s power functions

power.t.test(power = 0.80, delta = 0.5, type = "two.sample")   # sd = 1 by default, so delta = d: n = 64 per group
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 63.76576
##           delta = 0.5
##              sd = 1
##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.8
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
power.t.test(n = 200, delta = 1, sd = 5)                        # the simulation above: power about 0.51
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 200
##           delta = 1
##              sd = 5
##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.5140434
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
pwr.t.test(n = 100, d = 0.5, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")   # power about 0.94
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 100
##               d = 0.5
##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.9404272
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group
pwr.t.test(d = 0.2, power = 0.8, sig.level = 0.05)              # n about 394 per group
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 393.4057
##               d = 0.2
##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.8
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group

Case study (Potts et al., 2022, ACE-III). When a study compares cognitive scores between groups (dementia, mild cognitive impairment, controls), what sample size would it need to detect a small difference reliably? This is why power is planned before data collection.

2.4 The rundata tutorial

rundata <- read.csv("rundata.csv")
plot(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa6",
     xlab = "First run (km)", ylab = "Second run (km)")
reg1 <- lm(SecondRun ~ FirstRun, data = rundata)   # same as lm(rundata$SecondRun ~ rundata$FirstRun)
abline(reg1, col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)
title("Second run against first run")

coef(reg1)       # second run ≈ intercept + slope × first run
## (Intercept)    FirstRun 
##    4.674700    1.018939

The sheet’s title(“my title”) uses curly quotes; use title("my title"). Using data = rundata inside lm() is also better practice: predict() then works on new data.

Different graphs (statmethods.net)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
dotchart(sort(rundata$FirstRun[1:20]), main = "Dot plot (first 20)", xlab = "km")
barplot(colMeans(rundata), col = c("#cfdcf0", "#f6dcc0", "#cfe9de"), main = "Bar: mean per run", ylab = "km")
plot(colMeans(rundata), type = "b", pch = 19, xaxt = "n", main = "Line: mean per run", xlab = "", ylab = "km")
axis(1, at = 1:3, labels = names(rundata))
pie(table(cut(rundata$FirstRun, c(0, 20, 30, 40, 100))), main = "Pie: first-run bands")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Correlation

cor(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun)        # r = 0.976
## [1] 0.9762012
cor.test(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun)   # significant: p < 2.2e-16
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun and rundata$SecondRun
## t = 44.333, df = 97, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.9647003 0.9839856
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.9762012
round(cor(rundata), 3)                          # all pairs at once
##           FirstRun SecondRun FinalRun
## FirstRun     1.000     0.976    0.926
## SecondRun    0.976     1.000    0.961
## FinalRun     0.926     0.961    1.000

Which runs correlate the most? First and second (r = 0.976); runs further apart in time correlate less (first and final 0.926).

New column and subsetting

rundata$runDiff <- rundata$SecondRun - rundata$FirstRun     # improvement from run 1 to run 2

# How many ran more than 30 km in their first run?
y <- rundata$FirstRun[rundata$FirstRun > 30]
length(y)                                                   # 46
## [1] 46
sum(rundata$FirstRun > 30)                                  # shorter: TRUE counts as 1
## [1] 46
# How many did better in their second run?
length(rundata$runDiff[rundata$runDiff >= 1])               # the sheet's version: improved by at least 1 km (97)
## [1] 97
sum(rundata$runDiff > 0)                                    # strictly better at all (99)
## [1] 99
sum(rundata$runDiff < 0)                                    # worse (0)
## [1] 0

runDiff >= 1 counts runners who improved by at least 1 km, not everyone who did better. “Did better” is runDiff > 0. Here every runner improved.

Paired t-test

t.test(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun, paired = TRUE)
## 
##  Paired t-test
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun and rundata$SecondRun
## t = -23.986, df = 98, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -5.650776 -4.787204
## sample estimates:
## mean difference 
##        -5.21899

The same runners ran twice, so the test is paired: it tests whether the mean of the differences is 0. p is far below 0.05, so the second run was significantly longer, by about 5.2 km on average (95% CI in the output).

Exercise 3: Scientific notation

2.78e7 == 2.78 * 10^7          # TRUE
## [1] FALSE
format(2.78e7, scientific = FALSE)     # "27800000"
## [1] "27800000"
3.89e-7
## [1] 3.89e-07
format(3.89e-7, scientific = FALSE)    # "0.000000389"
## [1] "0.000000389"
t.test(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun, paired = TRUE)$p.value   # a tiny p-value in e-notation
## [1] 8.419286e-43
format.pval(1e-20)                     # how R reports very small p-values: "< 2.22e-16"
## [1] "< 2.22e-16"

A negative number after e means a small number (move the decimal point left); a positive number means a large one (move it right). When R prints a p-value like 8.4e-43, read it as 0.000…084 with 42 zeros after the decimal point: far below 0.05.

The tilde. In the sheets, ~0.0387 means approximately 0.0387. In R code, ~ means “is modelled by”: lm(SecondRun ~ FirstRun), boxplot(mpg ~ am).

4.1 The z-score method

standardUnits <- scale(heartRates)           # (x - mean) / sd for every value
summary(standardUnits)                       # mean 0; max 3.17 SDs above the mean
##        V1         
##  Min.   :-1.6836  
##  1st Qu.:-0.7556  
##  Median :-0.1005  
##  Mean   : 0.0000  
##  3rd Qu.: 0.7182  
##  Max.   : 3.1746
absoluteStandardUnits <- abs(standardUnits)  # ignore direction: count high and low together
outliers <- absoluteStandardUnits[absoluteStandardUnits >= 1.96]
length(outliers)                             # 15
## [1] 15
length(outliers) / length(heartRates)        # 3%, vs about 5% expected for normal data
## [1] 0.03
length(absoluteStandardUnits[absoluteStandardUnits >= 3])   # 3 extreme values
## [1] 3

4.2 The boxplot (Tukey) method

x <- boxplot(heartRates, main = "Heart Rates", col = "#cfdcf0", horizontal = TRUE)

x$out                                        # 138 137 139
## [1] 138 137 139
summary(heartRates)                          # Q1 = 67, Q3 = 94
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   50.00   67.00   79.00   80.84   94.00  139.00
IQR(heartRates)                              # 27
## [1] 27
upper <- 94 + 1.5 * 27                       # 134.5
lower <- 67 - 1.5 * 27                       # 26.5: the low fence
sum(heartRates >= upper)                     # 3 high outliers, matching the boxplot
## [1] 3
sum(heartRates <= lower)                     # 0 low outliers: the minimum is 50
## [1] 0

4.3 Look at the data too

hist(heartRates, breaks = 30, col = "#cfdcf0", main = "Heart rates", xlab = "bpm")

sum(heartRates == 50)                        # a suspicious spike at exactly 50
## [1] 27

Discuss: There’s a pile-up of values at exactly 50 bpm and none below. That looks like a floor: perhaps the device or the data-entry rule recorded anything lower as 50. Neither outlier method notices this, but it’s a data-quality problem (Week 1). Outlier rules flag candidates; deciding whether they are errors or genuine (an athlete’s heart rate, a tachycardia) needs domain knowledge.

Method Rule High outliers here
z-score, 1.96 |z| ≥ 1.96 15 values (high and low)
z-score, 3 |z| ≥ 3 3
Boxplot (Tukey) above Q3 + 1.5 IQR or below Q1 − 1.5 IQR 3 (137, 138, 139)

Summary of fixes to the sheets

Exercise Issue Fix
1 At i = 100 the sample is the whole simulated population Compare with mean(population), or sample from rnorm()
2 t.test(x, y, PAIRED = FALSE) paired is lower case; PAIRED is ignored
2 title(“my title”) straight quotes
2 “did better” = runDiff >= 1 that is “improved by ≥ 1 km”; use > 0
